evidence_2026.passage: The question is, John, we might anticipate versioned data package profiles. For example, GBIF requiring a Darwin Core data package with an occurrence table, among other tables of importance to its index, and so on. Might the Darwin Core maintenance group produce a registry of named profiles? If so, what might a governance structure look like for DP profiles? Checking. Yep, testing. A bit of background. There are no profiles now because our original pre-feedback was, "Please don't have more than one data model," and we took that seriously. So there is only one right now. So I think we might be heading in that direction, but we haven't talked about how such production would be proposed and managed. If I were to imagine, I would say that these would have to be incorporated as additional products for the standard. I don't know if everyone's familiar with what's in Darwin Core, what's not in Darwin Core. But recently, with our latest public review, schemas, some existing schemas, have been incorporated as part of the standard. This includes all of the GBIF-produced cores, occurrence event and taxon, plus several of the extensions that are obviously just simple Darwin Core type things. So measurement or fact, identification history, alternative identifiers, but not much beyond those things. Humble extension and chronometric age. But not, for example, the OBIS extended measurements or facts. Why? It seems obvious. Because we haven't had a conversation with OBIS to say if they want us to. Also, none of the GGBN extensions. evidence_2026.passage: Now I want to show you two very practical examples of data. How is it in Dino, and how can it be transformed into something in the Darwin Core data package format? This first example that you see here is a material sample, which represent actually a molecular sample that was extracted from something. So it has a parent material sample, a tissue sample preserved in alcohol, which in turn also has a parent material sample, which is a cataloged specimen of a fruit bat in a mammalogy collection. Now, what you see on this slide is really the same information as on the previous slide, but according to DINA's internal database schema, that's the upper and the left part of the slide. You will see again three blue boxes. They represent three material samples. They have a relationship between them via the parent material sample field, and we also have an organism with a determination in the scientific name. On the right lower part, you see how this data would be transformed in Darwin Core data package. And it works very well. Material samples just become material entities. We can model the relationships between them via the derived from material entity field. And that works very well. It just imposed some minor questions. For example, is it sufficient, like I did here, to link only the parent material sample of such a chain to the event where it was collected?

links.title: The conceptual model, presented with a design tool
links.then: John Wieczorek describes the proposed conceptual model as a semantic layer for Darwin Core classes.
links.now: John demonstrates the Data Package Designer and generating a descriptor from selected tables.
links.interpretation: The same speaker and standard connect a conceptual explanation with a concrete authoring demonstration in the later talk.
links.caveat: Tools already existed in 2025. This pair does not establish when the Designer was first built, or that authoring tools were absent before 2026.
links.review_notes: The 2025 passage describes a semantic layer; the 2026 passage describes selecting tables, inspecting relationships and generating data package JSON. The pair does not establish the tool’s creation date.
